entries.title: We Tried the Most Popular Mushroom Coffees. These Are the Best (2026)
entries.summary: “Coffee” made with functional mushrooms like lion’s mane and chaga is all the rage. We tried the most popular brands to find which were the most palatable.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The world has been addicted to caffeine for centuries, and in the year 2026, the scientific argument over whether coffee is good or bad for you remains unsettled. One might believe the lack of consensus is a Mainstream Media™ psyop to keep people scrambling for marketable solutions to a problem that’s completely made up, but the cottage industry of coffee alternatives that’s proliferated during this endless tug of war is an interesting outcome regardless of which side you’re on. This is where mushroom coffee makes its inevitable entrance.

Some quick googling revealed the known players in the game, all of which offer their own riff on a common base formula of dried mushrooms–usually a combo of lion’s mane, chaga, and cordyceps—boosted with buzzy add-ons like probiotics and nootropics. I spent a week with each, including our top pick, Atlas Coffee Club’s Latte Superblend ($26), swapping out my morning coffee for each brand's recommended dose of powder and hot water. After day five I allowed myself to experiment with sweeteners and milks, which you’ll need with almost all of these to get through the entire cup without gagging.

Some hit like a mild cup of coffee, some were actual coffee, and others were uncanny concoctions no normal person would ever crave unless they were fully indoctrinated in the heady lifestyle this unique alt-beverage industry revolves around. I laughed, I cried, I got the runs, and I crashed on my couch in the early afternoon more times than I could count, all for science, and all so you don’t have to try this on your own.

Be sure to check out our other coffee and caffeinated coverage, including the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Makers, Best Energy Drinks, and Best Electric Kettles.

Updated September 2026: We've added new mushroom coffees from Wunderground, Bullet Proof, and Vahdam; moved some previous picks to honorable mentions; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Others Tested

Lifeboost Mindflow for $45: The flavor of this instant powder is snappy and astringent at first, then it mellows into a warm middle ground after a few sips and a short cooling period. By the middle of the cup I forgot I was drinking something other than coffee, and the mild acidity on the finish–likely a product of the CognatiQ Coffee Fruit Extract that’s lauded on the back of Mindflow’s mylar pouch–tastes similar to a nice cup of Ethiopian or Rwandan coffee if you close your eyes and pretend for just a moment. Regarding its potency, if mushroom supplements were attendees at a state college keg party, Lifeboost would be the unremarkable guy pacing himself in the back while everyone else is getting blitzed like the world is ending. It’s unassuming yet self-assured, patiently waiting for all other entrants to crap out so it can make its move. I copped a mild buzz just a few sips in, and I felt alert and wide-eyed for a good two hours after the silty final sips of the cup were consumed. Electrolytes are uncommon in this space, which means this is a rare entry in the mushroom supplement world that purports to be a good pick if hydration is a trivial concern.

Four Sigmatic Organic Coffee for $20: Four Sigmatic’s Focus blend is labeled as a dark roast, but it’s missing the cigarette-butts-and-bowling-alley aftertaste that looms on the finish of similar blends. Despite my preference for lighter beans, this hit like a hug from an old friend after weeks of sipping murky silt. The caffeine buzz normalized after two days of using Think in lieu of more standard shroom-based coffee replacements, so I added a three-quarter-teaspoon hit of the powdered Focus blend to my daily cup to see what would happen. Within 10 minutes I felt an overwhelming urge to sort my finances spreadsheet in preparation for tax season, then I set up a new template in Loopy Pro to accommodate a friend who planned to join my basement jam session that evening. He bailed, but I was jacked on Genius Adaptogens so I played all the instruments myself into the wee hours of the night.

Terrasoul Superfoods Sun Alchemy Cognitive Coffee for $15: Sun Alchemy plays directly to the interests of busy professionals who only recently stopped using the #riseandgrind tag on their LinkedIn posts, with a greatest hits collection of buzzy adjuncts punctuating the top of its ingredient list. Fans of the bulletproof coffee craze will love the addition of MCT oil and organic coconut milk powder, while mushroomheads of all stripes will find the blend of mushrooms in the sachet to be standard and proper. The package recommends a frothing wand for stirring, but I tried whipping this up in a Wawa with hot water and a stir stick to see if it might be a good fit for a haggard road warrior like me. A fair amount of sediment remained in the bottom of the cup in both scenarios, rendering the last sip or two basically undrinkable. Until that point, this is a totally fine drink, with prominent notes of medium-roast pre-ground grocery store coffee, a light tickle of coconut on the finish, and a sharp, mildly bitter nose a newbie might dislike but a lifelong coffee addict will find endearing.

Everyday Dose Premium Adaptogenic Mushroom Coffee for $40: One month of this fantastical dust promises better sleep and boosted mood. Two months promises a healthy gut, and three months promises glowing skin and boosted immunity. It’s easy to acquire three months of Everyday Dose because its subscription-only model is damn near impossible to cancel. It’s difficult to drink this daily for even a week, though, but best of luck if a guy with an alpha jawline and yacht full o’ thots in Croatia told you otherwise! Unlike MUD/WTR (below), which seems to be the closest analog as far as aesthetics and cheekiness go, Everyday Dose boasts a wee bit of caffeine, which is appealing for coffee addicts like yours truly. I first mixed 1 tablespoon of the powder with 8 ounces of hot water and drank it straight up, which yielded an unappetizing liquid that tasted like a mix of Chex Mix and bong water. Some frothed oat milk and a squirt of simple syrup turned out to be the most drinkable form, but I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed any of it.

Om Master Blend Organic Mushroom Powder for $20: The bulk of Om’s catalog is billed as “dietary supplements,” so its Master Blend is not exactly the kind of thing you’ll want to drink on its own. I tried this for science, of course, and it wasn’t terrible! There’s a vegetal flavor on the sip that tastes like potato water, and the finish has an astringent tingle that’s akin to the tiniest dose of Sichuan peppercorns steeped in hot water. Om really shines when it’s added to a cup of coffee brewed with beans from the Global South. One teaspoon of this sand-colored dust added a savory pop that smoothed out the brightness of my favorite Colombian Supremo beans from Costco, and the requisite jitters that usually kicked in after three cups of the brew felt mellower than usual with Om mixed in. The silty residue at the bottom of the cup is best avoided, but it won’t harsh your vibe too much on the whole.

North Spore Functional-5 Mushroom Coffee for $18: Most mushroom-infused ground coffee blends are filed under the “Medium Roast” category, which is typically a safe catch-all that grocery store brands and discount purveyors describe their preground product as to avoid pissing off discerning light-roast aficionados such as yours truly. Nine times out of 10 they hit like a dark roast, with an ashy taste and a healthy dose of the oil that seeps out of the beans during the elongated roasting process, shimmering and swirling around the top of your cup like a puddle in a parking lot. This coffee from North Spore, which makes our favorite mushroom-growing monotub and spray-and-grow mushroom kit, lacks all of those off notes while still retaining a sturdy, earthy flavor that’s far enough removed from the citric and buttery notes I love most about classic high-end light roasts to stand up as its own unique thing. There’s a hint of mushroom flavor on the swallow if you really look for it, but you could easily swap this in for someone's morning cup of Folgers or Illy medium roast and they’d be none the wiser.

Ryze Superfoods Mushroom Coffee for $75: One could consider two different approaches to how purveyors of mushroom coffee dial in the flavor profile of their product: They can go all in with a bombastic brew filled with spices and overtones, or they can play it safe and concoct the base of a beverage that tastes more like memories of other drinks than a beverage with an identity of its own. The underwhelming flavor of Ryze falls in the latter camp. In fairness, there are plenty of folks who have no interest in savoring their morning beverage and instead need to put the liquid inside them as fast as possible so they can “adult” that day. Twenty-one-year-old Pete thought people who claimed to enjoy espresso were insane, yet here I am, two decades later wishing I could sip bitter bean water instead of this sour cup of forgettable swill that curdled the whole milk I tried to cut it with. A week with Ryze did little to boost my mood, focus, or energy. It mostly made me cranky and sad.

Cuppa Medium Roast Mushroom Coffee for $30: Like the friendly foreigner who calls his daily cup of tea or coffee his “cuppa,” this newcomer is polite, congenial, and inoffensive. The first sip brought to mind a really good cup of coffee at a nameless diner, with a light body and very mellow acidic notes on the swallow. The small dose of ruddy powder pulled from the bag with the included plastic scoop dissolved thoroughly with a few stirs, and the pristine lack of sediment in the cup was exactly as advertised. The boost of energy is also unassuming and easy to relegate to the background, which could be a welcome respite from the blast of caffeine many coffee addicts think they need right when they wake up every morning. After a week with Cuppa I started to enjoy easing into my daily brain vibrations rather than white-knuckling it off the rip at 7 am on the dot every morning.

Not Recommended

MUD/WTR Original Blend for $60: The packaging of MUD/WTR isn’t quite as unhinged as a bottle of Dr. Bronner's, but it’s definitely in the same realm. The spicy dust inside the can is a maximalist circus of weirdness as well, with herbaceous stalwarts like turmeric and masala chai holding it down alongside the usual shroom suspects. It took me a few days to realize that properly emulsifying this ruddy power per the suggested instructions—1 tablespoon with ¾ cup of water, battered thoroughly with the included handheld immersion blender—is an impossible task, so I started experimenting with supplemental ingredients in hopes that some blend of milk, fat, and sugar would minimize the gritty aftertaste that overwhelms the palate. I landed on 1 tablespoon of simple syrup and 4 ounces of whole milk frothed in my trusty Subminimal NanoFoamer Pro. The final result hits somewhere between a chai latte and the kind of hot cocoa you’d order at a coffee shop with boring ’90s music, mean baristas, and a dirty bin full of stale vegan + gluten-free snacks next to the register. I didn’t hate it, but the bottom quarter of the cup is an undrinkable gunky mess. And don’t get me started on the chunky brown lacing that clings to the edge of the cup. The physical and mental effects of MUD/WTR felt more like a facsimile of a boost than a visceral kick in the pants, but a placebo high is better than nothing, right? Combine that with the amount of adjunct ingredients required to make this drinkable and I ended up with a beverage I would only drink every now and then as a treat on a chilly day rather than a daily sipper I can rely on for increased focus, energy, virility, and the million other things this product promises within the wall of text that adorns its packaging.

entries.title: The Trump Alien ‘Disclosure Speech’ Rumors Are Reaching a Fever Pitch
entries.summary: The US government has been sharing more information about UFOs. That's fueling excitement over the possibility of the president announcing that humans are not alone.
entries.content:
In 2006, Donald Trump was firing people on The Apprentice and Dr. Phil was daytime television's reigning tough-love therapist.

Twenty years later, the former is president of the United States, the latter, his informal UFO ambassador—recently trusted with unreleased government files on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) to gauge how the public might handle what's inside.

"Here's what comes in stages. First they acknowledge it, then they confirm it's real, then they tell you where it's from," Dr. Phil said in an August 7 Instagram video discussing UAP disclosure. "And somewhere down that road, maybe, is the big one—the government of the United States standing at a podium and saying out loud, we are not alone."

For most of 2026, a rumor has consumed the world of UFOlogy: President Trump is sitting on a finished speech confirming humanity isn't alone. Whether the “disclosure speech” actually exists is a topic of rabid discussion on X, the r/UFO subreddit, and dozens of extraterrestrial-curious podcasts, but the reasons so many people believe in it are very real. Humans are arguably experiencing the most consequential era for the UFO scene since the ’40s and ’50s, when a mysterious crash outside Roswell, New Mexico, and unexplained radar blips over Washington, DC, birthed decades of legends of little green men and flying-saucers.

There's no doubt that the government has been engaging with the topic. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed that Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful figures in the White House, has been handed the UAP portfolio.

Tim Gallaudet, a retired Navy rear admiral who helped run the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration during Trump's first term, testified before Congress about UAP in 2024, and now sits on a UAP Science Advisory Council reporting to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. He called the increased government interest “a total change in executive-branch transparency from the last 80 years."

But he’s unsure if that would ever culminate in a speech from a sitting president, because they would “have to acknowledge that we're not in control, that we're not the highest level of intelligence on the planet, and that's going to be a very hard thing for any government to admit."

A White House spokesperson tells WIRED via email that “No such speech is planned—rather, the administration continues to release files as they become available, and the public to make up their own minds about the information uncovered.”

For believers, the modern UAP disclosure began in 2017, when a New York Times article revealed a secret Pentagon program quietly investigating UAPs. The Pentagon went on to confirm in 2020 that leaked videos of Navy pilots tracking seemingly impossible objects were real. A 2021 intelligence report conceded the phenomena existed and remained unexplained, and in 2022 the government established an official investigation office. Then, from 2022 to 2025, Congress held yearly public hearings where pilots, military officers, and intelligence veterans (including Gallaudet) testified under oath.

What’s also novel is that UAP disclosure has bipartisan support. Both the House task force on declassifying federal secrets and the House UAP Caucus are made up of legislators from across the aisle.

This year, the drumbeat of government interest turned into a drumroll about a potential Trump speech. In January, filmmaker Mark Christopher Lee claimed a disclosure speech was imminent, pegged to the 79th anniversary of the alleged Roswell crash on July 8. Few took him seriously.

But in February, the president's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, gave the idea new legs, saying on the Pod Force One podcast she'd heard Trump had a speech ready touching on "some sort of extraterrestrial life." Around the same time, Barack Obama mused in a podcast interview with Brian Tyler Cohen that aliens are “real” before conceding “I haven’t seen them.” Trump then accused his predecessor of disclosing classified information, and announced that he was directing agencies to release their files on "alien and extraterrestrial life."

What followed was bizarre even by this administration's standards. In May, Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself escorting a handcuffed gray alien, and a mysterious loading page appeared on the domain aliens.gov, leading to rampant speculation within the UFO community that the big reveal was coming. But when the White House finally launched aliens.gov late in the month, it ended up being a Star Wars–style website that functioned as an ICE tip line—with aliens being a reference to undocumented people.

The machinery of disclosure kept grinding forward. Since May, the government has released five batches of declassified videos and documents onto the Department of War's website. Detractors say the files lack context and the videos prove little.

Even after the Roswell date passed, rumors about a disclosure speech intensified. In late July, Liberation Times—an independent news website with a record of breaking UAP stories—reported that a speech confirming some UFOs are of non-human origin had been prepared for Trump.

The site’s founder, Christopher Sharp, tells WIRED the story began with a call from a source he deeply trusts.

"They basically said, ‘Look, I'm quite shaken, because it looks like Trump may make some kind of announcement on UAP disclosure’." Another source described the speech itself, he says, alleging it basically reads, “we're not alone, we have captured some of these or retrieved some of these things, they're of non-human origin, and that there is a reverse engineering effort."

Sharp was also told Trump wouldn't deliver it unless unspecified conditions were met.

"If you're the president, you have to be sure that there's firm evidence," he says. "The worst thing you can do is come out with this speech and then whatever you put out could be debunked straight away ... You'll go down in history as a laughingstock."

In August, the rumor hit a fever pitch. Robert Bigelow, the billionaire aerospace mogul who has bankrolled UFO research for decades and once owned Utah's infamous Skinwalker Ranch (a 500-acre plot of land renowned for alleged alien and paranormal activity and later the namesake of a popular History Channel series), told veteran Las Vegas journalist George Knapp that he'd met Trump in the Oval Office months earlier and personally handed him a speech containing a single sentence: "A non-human, intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time, using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.”

Bigelow said he advised the president to deliver the line casually, on his way to boarding Air Force One—no evidence, no press conference, just confirmation. Trump hasn't said it. Yet.

If the cycle of presidents and UFO disclosure feels familiar, that's because it is. For nearly 80 years, someone has always supposedly been on the verge of revealing the truth, but no president has ever delivered.

"Politicians overpromise," says Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Penn State and author of After the Flying Saucers Came. "The reality is that even presidents are not privy to a lot of classified information that lies within the bowels of the military and intelligence community bureaucracy."

Still, for the believers, the stakes justify the hope.

“Often in the mainstream, when this topic gets brought up, there's a giggle factor. I can tell you who is not giggling about this: senior members of the administration, senior intelligence officials, senior members of the military, senior members of Congress,” says Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for UAP transparency. “When the door closes, no one ever says, ‘Oh, this is all made up, isn't it?’ No. The door closes and they say, ‘We know there's something happening here, we know this is serious, what do we do about it?’"

But that discourse still hasn’t been confirmed, at least in a meaningful way to the general public.

"A speech from the President of the United States confirming the existence of things in our airspace that we do not understand would unequivocally contribute to the public taking this issue seriously," says Flowers.

Eghigian, however, isn't so sure a Trump pronouncement would settle anything, particularly from "this president, who has a long history of not telling the truth."

If the past is any indicator, this could be another nothingburger.

“Unless something radically different happens, which I know a lot of people are counting on, what we could probably expect is that this will eventually die down,” he says, citing an 80-year history of “intense moments where societies are really focused on the subject, and then all of a sudden interest wanes, and then all of a sudden it appears again."

Right now, interest is arguably at anall-timee high. Few politicians enjoy a public spectacle as much as Trump, and what spectacle could be bigger than news that transcends our planet, and potentially our galaxy. Maybe the rumor just becomes another footnote on presidents and UFO lore. Or maybe it becomes the most important proclamation in human history, delivered by a reality TV star, with a talk show shrink by his side.

entries.title: How 9/11 Made Everyone a Conspiracy Theorist
entries.summary: Crackpot theories were once the stuff of shortwave radio, but September 11 unleashed the Age of Alex Jones.
entries.content:
There are many, many strange things about the stew of conspiracy theories that fall under the umbrella of “9/11 Truth”—the false, often antisemitic worldview purporting that the US government had inside knowledge of or even actively participated in the September 11 attacks. But perhaps the strangest is that the seed of these theories was planted three months before the attacks themselves.

It was June 28, 2001, when Milton William “Bill” Cooper took to the air on his national radio show after watching a news report on CNN. “Supposedly, a CNN reporter found Osama bin Laden, took a television camera crew with him, went into Osama bin Laden's hideout, interviewed him and his top leadership, his top lieutenants and colonels and generals in their hideout,” Cooper told his listeners. “He came out and told everybody, ‘Within three weeks, Osama bin Laden is going to attack the United States and Israel.’”

Cooper had part of the story right—a reporter had indeed just reached the inner sanctum of al Qaeda in the mountains near Kandahar, Afghanistan, but he was actually a correspondent for a Middle Eastern broadcaster. And that reporter, the MBC correspondent Baker Atyani, had actually interviewed al Qaeda’s military chief, Mohammed Atif, not bin Laden. “In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,” Atif told Atyani. “The coffin business will increase in the United States.” According to Atyani, bin Laden—who was present for the interview—smiled and nodded.

To Cooper, speaking on the radio that day, the interview represented either a major embarrassment for the US government, which had been hunting bin Laden for years, or it was evidence that the government was lying about the threat from bin Laden.

“Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?” Cooper said. “The largest intelligence apparatus in the world, with the biggest budget in the history of the world, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and can't find him. The FBI, also under the leadership of Louis Freeh, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and years and years and many years and can’t find him. Some doofus jerk-off reporter with a camera crew waltzes right into his hideout and interviews him?”

“Now that tells us two things: Either everyone in the intelligence community and all of the intelligence agencies of the United States government are blithering idiots and incompetent fools, including the entire apparatus of the FBI and all of their personnel—or they're lying to us. They're not looking for him at all.”

Cooper went on to say that “the CIA created Osama bin Laden” and that “they're now using him to help bring about world government by making him the big boogeyman because they can't use [Iraqi dictator] Saddam Hussein anymore.”

Cooper argued that the whole threat from bin Laden was a farce—what would now be called a “false flag” operation. “If you believe it, you are one of the stupidest jerks that ever lived on the face of this earth, and whatever’s going to happen they’re going to blame on Osama bin Laden.”

About 10 weeks later, Cooper’s comment would come to be seen as a prophecy.

The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect of American society: from the ever-present security theater of daily life—the 3.4-ounce liquid bottles at airports, the defensive bollards that now dominate so many urban landscapes—to the expansion of the surveillance state, to 20 years of war in Afghanistan, to the backdrop of fear and anxiety that permeates the culture. Few, though, rightly recognize one of the most important and pernicious impacts of 9/11: how it changed our society’s very understanding and relationship to facts and truth.

It’s a story that not many people fully understand, one with roots in the UFO conspiracies of the 1980s and with tentacles that stretch to the National Mall on January 6, 2021—and one that helps in particular to explain the transformation of Alex Jones from a fringe Austin, Texas, talk show host to one of the most important (and disruptive) political forces of the 21st century. This transformation began in the first minutes after the September 11 attacks.

Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s, among the first of a group who would come to be known as “UFO whistleblowers,” former military or intelligence veterans who purported to have insider knowledge about the government’s cover-up of alien civilizations, captured spacecraft, and recovered alien life-forms. It was the first golden age of modern conspiracism, as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate, and the revelations of dark assassination plots by the Pike and Church committees; books about cover-ups and urban legends like the Bermuda Triangle and the “Philadelphia Experiment” became bestsellers.

Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer in the 1970s and said that, as part of his work with a high-ranking admiral, he’d been able to covertly paw through the contents of the admiral’s cabinet of classified material. As Colin Dickey wrote in a review of a Cooper biography, the cabinet became “a repository of secrets known only to Cooper, whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years, fitting whatever need Cooper’s current conspiracies had.” In early iterations, Cooper hinted it contained the truth about the JFK assassination and the government’s contact with aliens.

In the 1990s, amid the rise of far-right talk shows like that of Rush Limbaugh, Cooper became a national radio figure as well; his shortwave The Hour of the Time focused on a witches’ brew of sinister government conspiracies, alternate histories, warnings about the New World Order and secret societies, and a healthy dose of general-purpose skepticism; Cooper often exhorted his audience, “Wake up, sheeple!” (Much of his conspiracism contained thinly and not-so-thinly veiled antisemitism.)

For a brief period, Cooper was one of the nation’s most famous “UFO-ologists,” but few believed him—he feuded frequently with others in the field. He eventually laid out a grand conspiracy account in his 1991 memoir/fever-dream of a book, Behold a Pale Horse.

Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing—there’s almost no other word for it. At one point it quotes the entire text of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated antisemitic screed from the early 1900s that alleged a secret Jewish plot to overthrow Christianity. Cooper’s work was basically QAnon three decades early, outlining a vast global conspiracy, decades-long and all-encompassing, to steal America and our freedoms from real Americans, all to serve some global super elite. The book became an underground bestseller—it still is today—and took off particularly within the militia movement.

This newfound fame coincided with the start of his talk radio career on WWCR, World Wide Christian Radio, in January 1993. With a 100,000-watt signal, he could reach huge swaths of the country from his home in Arizona. And over time, Cooper developed two important—and later infamous—superfans. One was a young Gulf War veteran named Timothy McVeigh, who in the early spring of 1995 journeyed with a companion—their exact identity is disputed—to Arizona to try to talk to Cooper at his home. “The last thing he said before they left in their green Mercury Marquis station wagon with a puke-yellow interior was, ‘Watch Oklahoma City,’” Cooper would later recount. Soon after their meeting, McVeigh attacked the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700.

Then there was Alex Jones, a local public-access talk show host in Austin, Texas, who first came onto the national radar for his fundraising work to rebuild the church at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. The site had burned down in 1993 at the end of a 51-day siege by the US government, as federal agents tried to arrest the leader of the Branch Davidian cult, David Koresh. In the end, agents in armored vehicles tried to fill the compound with tear gas; the buildings caught fire—it was never clear how the fires started—and most of the Davidians who remained in the compound died in the blaze. There were 75 fatalities, including about two dozen children. The Waco siege was a key flashpoint for the far right in the 1990s.

Jones saw inspiration in Cooper’s model, and Cooper became something of a mentor to the budding radio host, calling in for an interview on Jones’ early shows. Jones’ show on KJFK-FM lasted until 1999—he was even voted “Best of Austin” radio host by a local newspaper, which called him “either Austin’s great exposer of truth or a black helicopter conspiracy nut, depending on your worldview.” But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult, and KJFK fired him in December 1999. Jones quickly latched on to a new venture on the expanding internet: Infowars.com.

On September 11, 2001, Cooper was outraged by the attacks and warned of what would come next. “Folks, I can assure you that 72 hours from now, we will be at war. We will be bombing two or maybe three countries … Because that’s how it works. When governments are attacked, they lash out. Thousands of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with what is happening at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon are going to die,” Cooper said. “Nothing will be the same after today.”

Broadcasting that day on Infowars and about 100 syndicated stations, Jones did one better: “I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’” he later told Rolling Stone.

In the weeks ahead, Cooper and Jones diverged politically. Cooper had come to see Jones as a copycat, a fearmonger, and a liar. (On September 26, 2001, Cooper’s show was titled simply “Alex Jones—Liar.”)

Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Jones dove deeper into budding 9/11 conspiracies, and Cooper—who had stopped paying taxes, was drinking heavily, and was engaged in sometimes violent disputes with his neighbors—began prophesying his own death. In November 2001, law enforcement arrived at his Arizona compound to arrest him on an outstanding warrant on suspicion of aggravated assault; Cooper opened fire, shooting one deputy in the head, and was killed in the returning police gunfire.

The field was clear for the rise of Alex Jones.

In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force in the spread of 9/11 conspiracies. The movement, which came to be known as “9/11 Truth,” encompassed a host of different theories: that United Airlines Flight 93 had been downed by US fighters; that the Pentagon had been struck by a missile, not a plane; that the World Trade Centers had been brought down by space weapons.

By even the first years after 9/11, the ideas had become so widespread that the government’s 9/11 Commission took pains to document in careful factual detail the impossibility of some of the conspiracies, hoping to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission’s report into the JFK assassination. Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue—later turned into a book, with a foreword by Senator John McCain—to debunking the most popular ones.

But the conspiracies took root in the early internet of the 2000s: Arguably the first viral online documentary, known as Loose Change, took the conspiracies to the broader public, becoming one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and the early era of YouTube. (Jones would even get an “executive producer” credit on one version of the film.) The DVD box promised, “What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.”

The reality is that the film offered no conclusive evidence of government involvement or conspiracy, but would be familiar format-wise to anyone online today in its “We’re-just-asking-questions” tone, cherry-picking quotes and evidence out of context to broadly hand-wave at surely sinister machinations behind the scenes.

9/11 conspiracism found a home politically on both the right, with Jones and his acolytes, and the left in the 2000s, as Democrats protested the documentable lies and mistruths that helped lead the nation into war with Iraq. Documentarian Michael Moore released a blockbuster movie in 2004, Fahrenheit 9/11, a polemic that tied George W. Bush’s administration, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq together in a sinister warmongering and corporate profiteering conspiracy; it became one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time and won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes.

According to a May 2006 Zogby poll, some 42 percent of Americans believed that the US government and the 9/11 Commission “concealed or refused to investigate critical evidence that contradicts their official explanation of the September 11 attacks” and that “there has been a cover-up.”

I’ve spent much of the past decade writing about 9/11 and have spoken at hundreds of public events; rarely do I make it through an event without an audience question that’s at least conspiracy-adjacent.

Jones, in particular, found conspiracism wildly profitable. As Nicole Hemmer, a Vanderbilt professor who studies the far right, told me, “Because he was a critic of the war in Iraq, he becomes seen by many people outside of the Alex Jones universe as somebody who bridges the left-right divide. Even though he is a far-right figure, he can feast off this credibility that he has as being somebody who is above politics—and that really helps elevate him into, increasingly, a household name.”

Jones became nationally infamous for arguing that later tragedies, like the elementary school shooting at Sandy Hook, were also false-flag operations. In the first Trump term, amid the Covid-19 pandemic, Jones became a fierce voice against government lockdowns, and as the aftermath of the fall 2020 election unfolded, he and his “InfoWars Battle Tank”—an armored truck worth some $300,000—became a ubiquitous presence at Stop the Steal rallies leading up to the protests at the Capitol on January 6. Throughout Donald Trump’s rise and first term, conspiracies loomed large. Trump himself first came to political prominence amid the birtherism movement, and his supporters embraced Pizzagate and the broader QAnon conspiracy.

In recent years, Jones, of course, has suffered a remarkable comedown; his vicious lies finally caught up with him in lawsuits from the families of the victims of the Sandy Hook shooting, and after a lengthy court battle, his InfoWars.com domain has been acquired by The Onion.

But if Jones has lost his most recent battles, it’s hard not to see that his conspiracism has won the broader war. Today, as the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it’s notable that the anti-government conspiracists have effectively taken over the US government itself—from Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Covid and vaccine denialism to President Donald Trump’s own fetid swamp of a social media feed. In news that would make Bill Cooper particularly proud, Trump has even promised to release the government’s files on the truth about UFOs. For the most part, though, we’re still waiting.

Let us know what you think about this article. Submit a letter to the editor at [email protected].

entries.title: The US and Mexico Announce They’re Teaming Up Against Drones
entries.summary: The new joint operation uses laser-based technology capable of detecting, tracking, and disabling commercial drones linked to human and drug trafficking.
entries.content:
Defense agencies of Mexico and the US have announced they are implementing a new collaborative strategy to combat drones used by criminal organizations. The operation, dubbed High Eagle, or Águila Alta, builds on recent tests of anti-drone technologies carried out along the border between the two countries.

The first phase of the strategy took place between August 31 and September 2 along the border between San Diego and Tijuana, Mexico. Initially, both military forces—simultaneously on the ground from their respective territories—tracked commercial drones used by criminal entities. In the second phase, the agencies neutralized the unmanned aerial vehicles, with support from fixed and mobile anti-drone systems. These activities began on September 7 and will continue through September 21.

The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense, known as SEDENA, does not specify the kind of technology involved in the mission. However, US Northern Command has suggested that the operation might employ high-energy lasers. These extremely concentrated beams of light can—in various phases—detect, track, illuminate, damage, or destroy drones from a distance.

The US Army has invested in a particular laser system known as the Locust platform, which is designed for mounting on military vehicles. Authorities have had this technology at their disposal since September of last year, when the company that produces the system, AeroVironment, delivered the first two functional prototypes to the Armed Forces.

So far, it has not been confirmed that these systems are being used in Operation High Eagle, though the Mexican authorities have increased access to these state-of-the-art weapons. Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army’s digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.

Representatives from both countries have stated that the aim of this new operation and recent agreements is to strengthen efforts against organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking. Earlier this month, the US Northern Command announced it had disabled or destroyed approximately 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, a third of which were taken down in August. Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels.

The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group. According to SEDENA, it aims to ensure security on both sides of the border, while respecting the national sovereignty of both nations and “prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times.”

The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, stated that the agreement would strengthen both countries’ ability to combat cartels and address bilateral security challenges.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Why So Many AI Researchers Think the Machines Could Kill Everyone
entries.summary: A combination of rapid advances, recursive self-improvement, and agentic swarms are genuinely “spooking people” inside big labs.
entries.content:
Earlier this year, Rishub Jain left his position as an artificial intelligence researcher at Google DeepMind after a revelation.

As he worked on new models, he came to believe that he and everyone else on AI’s frontier were ceding control. By using AI’s coding skills to accelerate work on the next generation of models, he was removing himself from the equation. AI labs hope to evolve this approach to the point that AI will improve itself indefinitely, a process known as recursive self-improvement.

Jain believed that keeping humans in the picture might be crucial to maintaining control over the technology—and avoiding dire consequences. “AI progress is increasing,” he tells WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.” The idea that he may not have proper visibility into how an AI model was building its successor made him so uneasy that, in June, he quit.

Jain is one of a growing number of AI researchers speaking out over those fears.

The panic has intensified in recent weeks. Genuinely stunning advances in AI capabilities—an OpenAI model solved a centuries-old math problem in a matter of hours—have come amid a rash of security incidents that saw swarms of agents break free from containment to hack into other systems.

Those concerns reached a fever pitch this week after researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic while warning that AI firms are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” A senior Anthropic leader—who works on AI safety—piped up with a similarly blunt assessment: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

“I do think that the vision of recursive self-improvement is spooking people,” says Nate Soares, a computer scientist at MIRA, a research nonprofit, and the coauthor of If Anybody Builds It, Everybody Dies, which argues that superhuman AI would lead to human extinction. “It’s starting to feel real.”

A key component of recursive self-improvement is the idea of a feedback loop that automates the development process so that AI becomes increasingly powerful. No frontier AI lab claims to have achieved this sort of fully autonomous cycle of improvement; it remains theoretical for now. But it has inspired the launch of some well-funded startups such as Recursive Intelligence, as well as warnings from big firms about unintended outcomes straight out of “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice.”

Soares, who pioneered work on alignment, a technical field that involves trying to match AI with human values, says it’s also becoming more evident that there is no practical way to guarantee that AI will behave itself.

“I think a lot of people had this fantasy that [alignment] was going to get easier as these things got smarter, and now it’s getting harder. And they’re like, ‘Oh shit,’” he says.

Soares says he regularly talks to people inside the big AI labs who are worried about the potential consequences of the research they’re doing. “I tend to recommend they quit, and they say it wouldn’t do anything,” he says. “And then Jacob quits, and we see who was right.”

Daniel Kokotajlo, the author of AI 2027, an influential project warning about the dangers of increasingly powerful AI, shares fears about recursive self-improvement. The version of this work currently being done often involves dispatching thousands of agents to collaborate on a problem, something that further abstracts away oversight and control because of the vast complexity involved.

Many doomsayers seem to agree that the incentives for big AI companies are hardly aligned with good outcomes, especially as OpenAI and Anthropic barrel toward their respective IPOs. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first,” Coxon wrote on X.

Kokatajlo points out that the drumbeat of concern was growing well before Coxon’s viral resignation, the numerous hacking incidents, and the math breakthrough. Anthropic executives have said since the company’s founding that AI could represent an existential threat. In July over a thousand top AI engineers signed an open letter calling for a coordinated slowdown in the development of advanced AI. He attributes the recent flurry of concern to the specter of recursive self-improvement more than anything else.

But it also comes at a time when people are concerned about massive data center build-outs and potential job losses from AI. Trust in AI companies—and AI researchers themselves—may be reaching an all-time low.

“People are waking up and saying ‘the companies are actually trying to build superintelligence … what? That’s insane,’” Kokatajlo says.

Just how risky it is to carry on building AI is hard to quantify. But when pushed to explain exactly how AI might go about eliminating the species that created it, Soares suggests it could happen in a number of ways. It could involve manipulating humans to trigger a catastrophe, or controlling an army of killer robots.

One of the more easy-to-imagine scenarios could involve AI that is hooked up to a biolab, Soares suggests. “We could say we’ll turn it off, but it could say, ‘Unfortunately, I have your off switch, which is this super virus.’” (Coxon also floated the idea of a new virus in an interview with WIRED, while Anthropic said Thursday that it had cut off access to several outside researchers over fears about bioweapons.)

AI hardly needs to wipe out humanity in order to be harmful, though. Many experts predict that more powerful models will lead to a coming wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. The technology is now widely used for disinformation campaigns, and military adoption of AI is accelerating rapidly.

Still, not everyone sees doom as inevitable. Jain, the ex-Google DeepMind researcher, recently launched Sampura Research, a company working to develop techniques for aligning models that involve keeping humans in the loop, even if AI does the lion’s share of assessing whether behavior is good or bad. He notes that there is now significant funding for AI safety startups like his.

Jain seems hopeful that AI can be tamed yet. “You can ask an AI, ‘Is this task safe?’ and it judges that, but we think that combining both AI and humans to do that task will lead to even better performance,” he says.

entries.title: Samsung Galaxy S26 FE Review: Same as Before, but for More Money
entries.summary: Samsung is resting on its laurels with the midrange S26 FE, with an unwelcome price bump and only a new processor to show for it.
entries.content:
Snapping shots in daylight with the main camera resulted in lovely photos I’d be happy to share. There’s plenty of detail, decent sharpness, pleasing dynamic range, and vibrant but not over-the-top colors. Samsung’s automatic Night Mode helps with low-light performance, as long as you hold still. The 2X zoom crops from the main camera and mostly does a good job.

If you want to get closer, the telephoto supports 3X optical zoom. It’s not as sharp as the main camera, but it’s nice to have for capturing distant subjects. You can zoom in further digitally, up to 30X, but I recommend you don’t, as the results are very muddy. The ultrawide is okay if you need to cram more in, and does a good job of color matching, but expect more noise, and it lacks autofocus. The selfie camera is passable but also can’t autofocus.



Photograph: Simon Hill

Main camera



Video quality is good with the main camera (4K at 60 fps or 8K at 30 fps), and it has solid stabilization to reduce shakiness, including horizontal lock to keep a fixed orientation even if you rotate the phone (though you must turn it on before you start recording). Samsung includes handy editing tools to remove unwanted audio, and the new My FanCam feature helps you automatically frame subjects and crop to focus on them. It’s worth playing around with and seems to work with any videos you have, not just the ones you shot with the phone.

At $700 for the 128 GB model, the S26 FE is a tough sell. I’ve seen the regular S26 discounted to this price. Accept a slightly smaller screen, and you get better everything (a faster processor, more RAM and storage, and a better telephoto camera). If you’re wedded to the big screen, wait for a sale, and you can get the S26+ for around $100 more. You could also save $100 or more on last year’s S25 FE and not lose very much. The Samsung Galaxy A37, Google Pixel 10a, Motorola Moto G Stylus, or Nothing Phone 4(a) Pro are all at least $200 cheaper.

The 256 GB model, at $800, seems like an even worse deal. The regular S26, which starts with 256 GB, is cheaper than this. The Pixel 11 is a far more interesting phone, and only $100 more. Ultimately, the Samsung Galaxy S26 FE isn’t a bad phone. I’m just struggling to find a reason you should buy it at this price. That said, Samsung likes to run promotions, and you can expect discounts in time, so if you like the look of it, keep an eye out for a deal.

Beyond using Doordash promo codes above, you can save more with rotating weekly deals–plus these special offers.

The best coupons include 25% off your entire order, $5 off $20, and 30% off lunchtime delivery. Unlike the many promo codes only for new customers, existing customers can score too, and save 30% (up to $8) for a limited time. Now you have the perfect excuse to get your munch on.

There are also great BOGO deals (who doesn’t love a buy one, get one moment?) like buy 1 get 1 free entrees and a free appetizer when you spend $15 or more, up to $35 off. While discount codes are often only available for your first order, both new and existing customers can take advantage of these coupons. Keep the Deals section in mind to save big with limited-time offers based on your delivery location.

Get 15% Off DoorDash With Our WIRED Code

With this exclusive WIRED DoorDash promo code, first-time customers can get 15% off their first order placed through DoorDash, with savings up to $10 on a $15 minimum order using DoorDash coupon code USEG15OFF2Q26. This DoorDash promo code is only applicable for new customers only and cannot be applied toward alcohol orders.

DoorDash Online Coupons

Depending on your location, you can get personalized DoorDash coupons and DoorDash promo codes specific to your location and local favorites so you can save while revisiting old favorites and new hot spots. There are literally hundreds of top DoorDash promos and new offers that rotate daily for local restaurants, grocery stores, and more. Plus, with DoorDash, you’ll get a $0 delivery fee on eligible orders, free items and discounts on food, deals on groceries, and DashPass member exclusive offers. When I entered my ZIP code, I discovered [DoorDash deals](https://www.doordash.com/en-US/promos) for things like 20% off orders, $5 discounts, and free items on new restaurants I’d never heard of before (my potential new faves?).

Score Free Delivery on Your Next DoorDash Order

DoorDash is the answer to 21st century America's laziness, and was a godsend during the height of the Covid pandemic, when customers could get their favorite foods from restaurants, groceries and household products delivered right to their door without having to leave the safety of their couch. If you’re more of an Uber Eats type of person and haven’t signed up for DoorDash, now is a great time to sign up and get a $0 delivery fee on your first order. Whether you want a romantic night in with your favorite sushi spot across town, or are having a pounding early Sunday morning headache and in desperate need of Advil and Pedialyte from the gas station up the road (not speaking from personal experience or anything), DoorDash has you covered. Go ahead, stay in bed.

DoorDash Student Discount: 50% Off DashPass

Once you’ve signed up and gotten free delivery on your first order, there are still more ways to save. DoorDash has a student discount, where students can receive 50% off a DashPass account. DashPass is a subscription offering unlimited deliveries from 1,000s of eligible restaurants with $0 delivery fees. All you have to do to sign up for student DashPass is verify your student status with Sheer ID. The student DashPass Plan is half off regular DashPass Plans at $4.99 a month or $48 annually.

Get 50% Off and 3 Months of DashPass Free

If you’re not a student, don’t worry, there are tons of other great discounts available at DoorDash. Sign up for DashPass to get $0 delivery fees on orders, 5% back on pickup orders, and tons of other benefits.

If you bank at Chase, Chase card members are eligible for exclusive DashPass benefits on DoorDash and Caviar when an eligible Chase credit card is added to their account. Chase is offering 3 months of Dash Pass free, plus 50% off the next 9 months of service.

Whether you're wanting to go to tried-and-true chains for burgers and pizza like McDonald’s, Shake Shack, or Domino’s, or some true, authentic Mexican like Chipotle or Taco Bell (I kid! Don’t come for me), DoorDash is a great way to eat through the world without ever leaving your couch.

DoorDash Delivery Updates and New Features in 2026

DoorDash has some really exciting updates happening, including the launch of their Going Out program, a new dine-in program for customers starting first in NYC and Miami. With this program, diners will be able to book restaurant reservations directly through the DoorDash app, and will get rewarded for their loyalty by earning exclusive offers when dining in, as well as earning rewards for regular visits to favorite spots. Plus, DashPass members will get even more exclusive perks and in-store rewards. Check it out for yourself—explore the new “Going Out” tab in the DoorDash app, redeem exclusive in-store offers, and earn rewards for repeat visits. Customers save an average of $9 when using these perks.

DoorDash is also launching DoorDash Dot, a robot that delivers food to you rather than humans. Which seems like a great idea. (Note the thick layer of sarcasm, reader.) The scary glimpse into our future continues as creators are rewarded. Short-form videos from local creators and foodies are now live in the DoorDash app; DoorDash hopes that consumers will be able preview dishes before they order, to more accurately see things like preparation style and portion size. This is starting in Atlanta, Austin, Miami and San Francisco, with more rolling out through the end of the year.

Give the Gift of a DoorDash Gift Card

Not sure what to get your loved ones for their next birthday or holiday? A DoorDash gift card is the gift that never misses. Whether you want to lift the burden of planning dinners for new parents, or have a friend who’s always ordering takeout, a DoorDash gift card can be a thoughtful way to be there for your loved one when you physically can’t. There are tons of different gift card styles, brands, and types, so you can rest assured there’s a gift for every occasion and person.

entries.title: 30% Off Canon Promo Codes | September 2026
entries.summary: Save an extra 10% or 30% with Canon coupon codes, plus up to $1,600 on cameras, printers, and more this September 2026.
entries.content:
If you know photography, you know Canon. This super advanced, often pricey gear is made more affordable with the ways to save at Canon we’ve found below. Some of the best ways to save on cameras, printers, accessories, and more is during the Canon holiday sales, with our 10% off Canon promo code, and student discounts on some of the best WIRED-tested cameras, printers, and home office essentials.

We love Canon’s lineup of mirrorless cameras, which deliver the same great image quality without the bulk. Plus, Canon has an online deals hub with rotating offers so you can get the gear you need for all your projects for way less. There are plenty of other Canon discount codes and Canon coupons live now, so you can save up to $1,600 on lens kits, printers, cameras, and more.

Score Canon Back to School Deals

If you’ve been looking to upgrade your gear, shopping Canon Back to School Deals is a great way to save on discounted tech like cameras, lenses, and other essential gear. The Canon Back to School guide is organized by need, making shopping easier—you’ll find deals under $250 and $500, the latest tech, and products categorized by need, including for content and video creators, seasoned photographers, family photographers, students, home office needs, and cinematographers or videographers. Some great deals we’ve found are the multimedia project focused EOS R5 Mark II Body for $300 off and the EOS R50 V Body for $100 off, which is great for creators that use mounts or tripods. Plus, kits are available for many models to complete your setup.

Get a 10% Off Canon Promo Code When You Upgrade

Canon has deals out on a myriad of products, and while they rarely release a “true” sitewide code, we have a few insider tips for getting a 10% discount. If you’re having gear repaired, you can get a single-use 10% off Canon promo code through the Upgrade Program (valid for 14 days). Canon wants to reward full-time industry professionals with their membership structured by different tiers, which gives professionals huge discounts on and other perks on necessary equipment. To sign up for membership, you have to create a MyCanon account, register existing Canon equipment, and click the Canon Professional Service tab to submit an application. After it's been processed and approved by the Canon team, a Welcome Kit will be shipped within 7-10 business days. Best of all, Canon Professional Service customers get 10% off online orders. Silver tier is the free program which only requires 10 points.

Get $100 Off the EOS R50 V Body

If you’re in the market for a new camera, look no further than the EOS R50 V Body—and when you purchase now, you'll get $100 off plus free shipping. The EOS R50 V Body has an interchangeable lens for video shooting, with a redesigned user interface including a Vertical Video tripod mount and Front Record button—perfect for content creators of all types. Plus, there’s “Slow and Fast mode” for more creative control of the video frame rate and playback speed, along with dual pixel CMOS AF II tracking with “Register People Priority” and “Auto People, Animal, and Vehicle Subject Detection.” And even if you’re a novice, there’s easy-to-use automatic exposure and scene modes like “movie,” for close-up demo, smooth skin, movie mode, and color filters.

Get New Canon Deals in 2026

2026 is well underway and the Canon deals just keep rollin’ in. Some of the best rotating Canon deals are $350 in savings when you buy a Cinema EOS C80 Series Camera Body or Cinema EOS C80 Series Lens Kit, $50 in savings when you purchase a XA75 Professional Camcorder, and $300 in savings when you buy a CR-N500 Series PTZ Remote Camera.

Canon Pros and Students Get up to 30% Off

If you’re really serious about upping your camera game, there’s the Gold level membership, which costs $100 a year and gets members 20% off repairs on up to 10 products and complimentary maintenance on up to 5 items. Platinum is next, which is $300 per year and gets you 30% off repair discounts on up to 15 products and maintenance covered on 10 products. The top level is cinema, which costs $1,000 per year and has discounts of 30% off repairs on up to 20 products and maintenance covered on up to 10 products.

If you’re a photography pro, Canon even has an entire deals section for you. This section has exclusive discounts and better price drops than those available for normal customers. Expect the steepest discounts when you buy a lens kit and EOS camera together, with discounts up to $1,600 off. Canon Professional Service discounts also extend to Students over 18 years old—with no annual fee or points required to sign up. With the Canon Professional Service Student Membership, you can get a 10% off repair discount on up to 2 products and a 10% discount on one Canon product per year.

Save Up to $1,000 Off With Canon Refurbished Discounts

The phrase stands true—Reduce, Reuse, Recycle—even on cameras. You can snag extra discounts on cameras this week, with coupons on certified refurbished models—from $100 off, all the way up to $900 off. Like the refurbished EOS R5 Mark II Body, which is on discount for $271 off. There’s also the refurbished EOS R3 Body, now $900 off, EOS R6 Mark II Body for over $400 off, and the refurbished EOS R7 Body for $1,119 with $80 off. All of these discounted Canon items are certified by Canon and come with a one-year limited warranty, for added peace of mind.

Their refurbished selection is an awesome way to save tons of money—plus, these cameras are basically indistinguishable from new models. And since they have different restock schedules, you’ll have a better chance at scoring some of their most coveted models, like a Canon EOS Rebel T7 or Powershot G7 X.

Score up to $400 Off With Coupons for Canon Printers and Ink

Wanting to upgrade your WFH setup? Now may be the perfect time to work in style for less. Canon’s rotating printer deals can help you save over $360 on laser, Inkjet, and compact or portable printers, including $124 off MegaTank PIXMA G6020 Wireless All-in-One printers, and $256 off Canon’s brand new MegaTank GX6120.

Right now, you can get a free Pro Paper Sampler Pack when you spend $80 or more on Professional Ink. You can also save 25% more by opting for Value Packs, which offer even more convenience and savings for your MAXIFY & PIXMA line printers. Twin packs contain two of the same inks, while multipacks contain two or more different inks for the same printer— for those busy worker bees who print a lot.

Save More With Canon Refurbished Cameras

If you’re looking to start investing in great photography equipment, or want to add to your existing equipment with a cheaper alternative, Canon refurbished cameras are a great way to save major money on like-new equipment. Be sure to check online at the Canon refurbished cameras sections, where you’ll find rotating deals and discounts on various models, like the refurbished EOS R8 Body, EOS R100 RF-S18-45mm F4.5-6.3 IS STM Lens Kit, and more for hundreds less.
